vignette:
Malik, a 21-year-old African American chef who worked the evening line at a busy downtown restaurant, described the assault as happening after a late shift when he was walking to his car in the staff lot. He had been cornered by a man he did not know, forced into a narrow space between parked vehicles, and assaulted while the sound of a car engine idling nearby and the sudden slam of a door seemed to freeze the moment in place. What stayed with him most was the loss of control: the sense that his body was being used against his will, that he could not make it stop, and that his own reactions in the moment did not fit who he believed himself to be. In the weeks that followed, ordinary moments began to carry the event back into his present with no warning. A car backfiring outside the kitchen, tires grinding in the alley, or someone stepping too quickly behind him in the prep area could instantly throw him into the full memory, not as a story but as an engulfing return. When that happened, Malik found himself on guard before he could think, scanning for danger, feeling his body tense, and immediately checking himself for signs of injury or threat. He would rub at his arms, chest, and neck as if making sure they were still intact, and when the memory hit hard he sometimes detached from it altogether, trying to push the scene away from his mind by going numb and blank.

His appraisals of the assault made these episodes harder to settle. Malik was haunted by the belief that he had acted in ways that went against who he was, and that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening. He spoke with shame about not having fought harder, and this belief fed a bleak conviction that he had no future. Those thoughts did not stay abstract; they made him more vulnerable to the same everyday cues that now felt loaded with danger, so that the sight of a vehicle idling outside his apartment, or a sudden movement in the kitchen, could trigger the same surge of alarm. The memory itself was also entangled with this self-blame. When he tried to explain what had happened, he repeatedly lost the thread and could not finish, as if the account broke apart under the weight of what he thought it meant about him. At moments when the memory broke through, he heard fragments in his head that seemed to belong to the assault - a door closing, a voice, the sound of an engine - and those intrusions made the event feel even more immediate and less narratable. The more he struggled to make sense of it, the more the scene returned in pieces, each fragment pulling him back into the same helplessness.

Over time, Malik tried to manage these reactions by living as if he could keep danger at bay through constant effort. He became vigilant everywhere, even inside his own home, and his apartment no longer felt restful; he would keep lights on, listen for noises in the hallway, and react as if danger were present even when nothing was wrong. At work, sudden movements from coworkers put him immediately on guard, especially in the tight, fast pace of the kitchen where bodies brushed past and pans clattered. Because the triggers were so closely tied to those moments, he began to build habits around them: he avoided certain routes to work when he thought traffic noise might unsettle him, and he watched cars with a fixed intensity that left him exhausted. Yet these strategies did not calm him for long. Detaching from the memories gave him a brief sense of distance, but it also left the scenes unfinished and more likely to return in fragments later. Constantly checking his body kept him focused on danger and injury, which only deepened the feeling that something was still wrong. Revenge fantasies, meanwhile, offered a private sense of power - he imagined getting even with the people responsible - but afterward he felt more ashamed and more convinced that he had been changed for the worse. Each attempt to control the fear seemed to circle back into the same memory, the same self-judgment, and the same sense that he could not trust his own mind or future.

By the time he came for help, Malik was sleeping poorly, bracing whenever a car passed his building, and dreading the busy, unpredictable movements of the kitchen. What finally pushed him to seek treatment was realizing that he was avoiding more and more of ordinary life just to keep from being pulled back into that night. He said he was most afraid that he would stay trapped in this state forever, reacting as if he were still in danger, and most hoping that someone could help him feel like himself again without the memory taking over every part of his day.
